text: Ensembles with different structures may encounter different group dynamics. <break time="0.8s" /> For instance, Ford and Davidson studied members of 20 professional and semi professional wind quintets in the United Kingdom. <break time="0.8s" /> The technique and timbres of the instruments of the wind quintet which typically comprises a flute, oboe, clarinet, French horn, and bassoon are more distinct than those of string quartets, and intragroup dynamics may be quite different from quartets due to the odd number of members. <break time="0.8s" /> Dynamics inherent in the way the music is scored afford greater opportunities for democracy within the group, such as more equality and interchangeability among musical parts for example, the flute is often assigned the melody, but sometimes also plays an inner part. <break time="0.8s" /> Unlike the more rigid string quartet, there is also more flexibility in seating arrangements for wind quintets. <break time="0.8s" /> In addition, although the flute player was most frequently named as the leader, members of wind quintets were less likely to identify a clear leader than members of string quartets in Murnighan and Conlons study. <break time="0.8s" /> Instead, Ford and Davidson noted that in most of the quintets, players took equal responsibility for leading the ensemble. <break time="0.8s" /> The musical structure and social structure of the group seem to reflect each other.
